source.title: One Language, Two Scripts: Probing Script-Invariance in LLM Concept Representations

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures script-invariance of SAE feature activations, not whether increasing SAE dictionary size splits features or any of the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported Jaccard results concern similarity across Serbian scripts and model scales. They do not test feature splitting, parent-child input partitioning, feature-family geometry, absorption, canonical units, or sparsity-objective artifacts. The script-invariance results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study measures Jaccard overlap of active Gemma Scope 2 SAE features (one width, 65k) across Serbian Latin/Cyrillic scripts. It never varies dictionary size or sparsity, never compares SAEs of different widths, and never examines parent/child latents, absorption or feature families. It uses SAEs as a tool and cites Bricken et al. only as background, so it bears on no version. The record's 'discusses' overstates the engagement: feature splitting is never discussed. The only nearby remark is a speculative aside that larger models may have 'finer-grained features', which concerns model scale, not SAE dictionary size.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Gemma Scope 2 SAE features are substantially script-invariant for Serbian, with script change causing less divergence than paraphrasing. They report that this invariance strengthens with model scale, and that SAE features capture meaning above surface tokenization.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates SAE feature-set similarity across scripts; it does not reproduce or compare a feature-splitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-script original similarity rises across model scales, while cross-script random similarity falls; cross-script cross-paraphrase similarities remain roughly stable across scales. Results are averaged across selected layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-3 models (270M–27B), the same Serbian sentence in Latin and Cyrillic activates overlapping 65k-width SAE feature sets. Cross-script original Jaccard rises from 0.501 to 0.649 with model scale, while the cross-script random control falls from about 0.42 to 0.21.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE active-feature sets are largely invariant to script (orthography) for meaning-matched inputs, and this invariance strengthens with model scale.

record.problems: The dataset has 30 sentence triplets and limited domain coverage; the study evaluates only the Gemma family with one SAE configuration. Results are averaged across selected layers, and the authors state that the analysis does not establish causal contributions of shared features.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B.2, Tables 3 and 4: within-language comparison results and the table-wide aggregate in Table 4 are omitted because the extracted rows focus on the reported cross-script and cross-language comparisons; Appendix B.1 and Table 1 aggregate results are not duplicated.

untested.parts: All of it: there is only one SAE width (65k), so no dictionary-size variation.
All of it: Gemma Scope 2 is an open release, but splitting is not measured in it.
All of it: no feature-family geometry or hierarchy analysis. The 'semantic hierarchy' phrase refers to an ordering of similarity conditions, not feature families.
All of it: no parent/child latent firing analysis and no size or sparsity sweep.
All of it: no cross-width latent decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
All of it: there is no comparison of training objectives.

record.verdict_notes: Row states of cannot_determine and versions ['none'] are appropriate for every row. The rows are transcribed correctly from Table 4. The single fixed SAE configuration (65k width, medium L0, threshold 0.1) rules out any splitting test. The authors' speculation about finer-grained features in larger models is an untested hypothesis, and it concerns model size rather than SAE dictionary size.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary SAE dictionary size or test whether larger-dictionary features split smaller-dictionary features.
It uses Gemma models at multiple model scales, but does not test splitting in large models or open SAE releases.
The study does not test nested feature families or whether split features form geometrically close concept hierarchies.
The study does not test parent-child latent firing, absorption, or effects of SAE size or sparsity on absorption.
The study does not compare larger and smaller SAE dictionaries for latent decomposition or novel latents.
The study does not test whether splitting is an artifact of the sparsity objective or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

relation.reason: The text cites Bricken et al. 2023 and Templeton et al. 2024, but only as SAE background. It never mentions feature splitting, absorption or feature families, so 'discusses' does not fit and cites_only is the right call.

tranche.reason: The study measures how well SAE features hold up across scripts (Jaccard overlap of active features) using one SAE width (65k). It never varies dictionary size or sparsity and never looks at parent/child latents, absorption or feature families. It neither tests nor uses feature splitting.

source_check.notes: Off-topic for feature splitting: one SAE configuration (65k width, medium L0, threshold 0.1) and no width comparison. Table 4 values are averaged over the tested layers and over 30 sentence pairs. The 'finer-grained features' remark (Sec. 4.2) is about model scale, not SAE size.
